title: Guanyin's chapter chanted (Kern ch. 24)
hookLine: this chapter is chanted alone across East Asia
tomorrow: The king and his sons (Kern ch. 25)

lines: A THIN BOOKLET ON A BENCH.
cards: On a temple bench, or at a small shrine on top of a kitchen cabinet, a few people sit with a thin booklet open and chant together. The booklet isn't the whole Lotus Sutra.
It's one chapter, yesterday's, traveling on its own. In Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese Buddhism, the universal gate is recited as a short scripture of its own.
You met Guanyin last year; this time, stay with yesterday's chapter, and listen to how it is used.

teach.h: A CHAPTER THAT BECAME A BOOK.
teach.b: First, a chapter that became a book. Printed and chanted on its own, it is often called the Guanyin Sutra in Chinese, and in Japanese the Kannon-gyo.
People recite it at home and in temples, in times of illness and fear, and on ordinary mornings. Second, the names. Guanyin is the Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara.
The fuller form, Guanshiyin, is the name in Kumarajiva's Chinese Lotus, and it is usually rendered: the one who perceives the sounds of the world.
In Japan the name is Kannon, in Korea Gwaneum, in Vietnam Quan Am. And here yesterday's many forms come back.
In Indian art the bodhisattva appears as a princely male figure; in Chinese art Guanyin is often shown as a woman in white robes.

Some Buddhists in these traditions say the same compassion takes whatever form people can receive. Third, the verses. The chapter closes with verses that retell its promises in rhythm, easy to carry in the mouth.
Someone pushed into a pit of fire calls the name, and the fire becomes a pool. Someone pushed off a mountain stays in the air, like the sun.

teach.h: VERSES OF FALLING AND BEING HELD.
teach.b: The verses are full of falling and being held.

The chapter is about a bodhisattva who hears. The people who chant it are calling out, and they are also practicing hearing: the sound in the room, the voices beside them, their own breath between lines.
Some who chant it describe this as being heard and learning to hear, in the same breath.

how: In Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese Buddhism, the universal gate chapter is recited on its own as a short scripture, and people call on Guanyin with the chant Namo Guanshiyin Pusa.

o: a chant used only at funerals in Japanese temples
a Chinese hymn composed long after the Lotus Sutra
the universal gate chapter, recited on its own as a sutra

games.q: Guanyin's chapter chanted: tap the pairs.
p: perceives the sounds of the world
becomes a pool in the verses

s: Guanyin and Avalokiteshvara are two unrelated figures
Guanyin is the Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of the universal gate.
the universal gate chapter is also recited on its own, apart from the whole sutra
it is often called the Guanyin Sutra in Chinese and the Kannon-gyo in Japanese.
the bodhisattva is shown the same way in every country
princely and male in Indian art, often a woman in white in Chinese art.

games.q: in the chapter's verses, someone is pushed into a pit of fire and calls the name of the one who hears. what happens?
o: the fire burns on, and they endure it
the fire is never mentioned again
games.why: the verses say the fire pit turns into a pool; the whole poem is full of falling and being held.

practice: If you chant, say Guanyin's name the way it is said in Chinese temples, Namo Guanshiyin Pusa, slowly, once on each out-breath; if you'd rather not chant a name, hum one long, low note instead. The sound is half the practice.
The other half is listening as it fades, all the way to silence, before the next breath.

wordCard.voice: Guanyin's chapter chanted. The universal gate chapter of the Lotus Sutra, recited on its own as a short scripture about the one who hears the world's cries. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: Guanshiyin, shortened to Guanyin; the name in Kumarajiva's Chinese Lotus for Avalokiteshvara.

carryVoice: Your line: chanted everywhere. One chapter, traveling on its own. Go gently.
